zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-checks used the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan-grounded readings and English review notes are this review's own work, not a replacement NINJAL transcription.

lines.note: Nanbocu combines south and north, explicitly unpacked as Minami and qita. It confirms that the preceding page's Nãbo- is a catchword anticipating this entry, not an additional body line.
Nanbôfodo asks 'how much' or 'what quantity'. The circumflex and the unexpanded abbreviation q̃ are retained, while Adu. identifies the expression as adverbial.
This Nancai is a dangerous sea, explained as Nanguino vmi. It is distinct from the homograph for the southern sea two rows later.
Adds 'troublesome' or 'arduous' to the dangerous-sea definition. The smudged interior of trabalhoſo does not require a different word.
The second Nancai means the southern sea, matching Minamino vmi. The printed comma after the headword is retained rather than harmonized with neighboring full stops.

runs.text: Caminho por mar pera as partes do

lines.note: Nancaidǒ is explained as a sea route toward the southern regions. The caron is visible, and the directional reference continues into the next row.

Locates those regions southward relative to the capital. The scan-compatible Miayaco is preserved despite its unusual vowel order; it is not silently normalized to Miyaco and is a Japanese place-term embedded in Portuguese.
This Nancu concerns a difficult saying or authoritative passage. Cataqi cu supplies the Japanese explanation; the nature of the difficulty follows below.
Completes the definition as something difficult to understand. The Portuguese spelling difficultoſa preserves both printed f letters and the long s.
A different Nancu denotes severe suffering. Enlargement supports curuximi, 'suffering', rather than OCR euruximi: the first letter has the open right side of c, consistent with the torment gloss.
Completes grandes tormentos, 'great torments'. It closes the suffering sense of Nancu, not the preceding difficult-text sense.
Nanda is equated with Namida, tears. The explanatory i remains part of the dictionary's apparatus and does not introduce a Portuguese sentence containing the Japanese synonym.
Nandai introduces a difficult subject or assigned theme. The printed Japanese explanation Catai arauaſu is retained without converting it into a more idiomatic modern paraphrase.

runs.text: ſa ſobre que ſe compoem verſos, ou cantigas.

lines.note: Completes difficultoſa and specifies a subject on which verses or songs are composed. Compoem is retained without supplying an unprinted accent.
Extends Nandai to a difficult or troublesome matter generally. The scan restores the full difficultoſa where OCR had broken the word into difficuli ſa.
Nandaiuo iycaquru illustrates imposing a difficult matter on someone. The historical verb spelling is retained, and its Portuguese object and elaboration follow on the next row.

runs.text: couſa de demanda, ou difficultoſa deſe execu-

lines.note: Continues the imposed matter as a dispute or something difficult to carry out. The close printed deſe is retained, and execu- continues into executar below.
Completes executar, 'to carry out', and closes the Nandai example. The short continuation is retained as its own physical row.
Nandemo nai is something of little importance or consequence. The second Portuguese noun, specifying little usefulness, follows on the next row.
Completes 'of little usefulness' and gives Nandemo nai coto, an insignificant matter. The printed example remains unexpanded despite having no separate translation.

This is the corresponding adverbial expression for the preceding insignificant or negligible sense. The narrow division in the supplied Nandemo nǒ is retained because the scan does not decisively exclude a space; the historical long-vowel form is not modernized to naku.
This Nanden is the southern sky, explained as Minamino tẽ. The final l of ſul is visible at the rule and restores a letter omitted by OCR; tẽ retains its nasal abbreviation.
A second Nanden describes a south-facing palace building. Minami muqino tonozzucuri is the Japanese explanation; i introduces a further equivalent on the next row.
Dairino goten identifies the imperial palace, glossed 'royal palaces'. The scan clearly supplies Dairino, correcting OCR Dairmno without changing its printed word division.

runs.text: Camara em que ſe dorme, & poem al-

lines.note: Nando is a chamber used for sleeping and keeping belongings. Al- begins algum across the line break; the room is not defined only as a modern storage cupboard.
Completes algum fato and names clothing among the stored belongings. Fato here belongs to the source's possessions/clothing vocabulary, not the unrelated modern sense 'fact'.

Nandogamaye is the raised construction or doorway made for access to the sleeping chamber. Obra is preferred to OCR Cbra for the weakly printed initial; the close portalmais join is retained rather than silently respaced.

runs.text: ſe faz pera entrar neſta camara de dormir.

lines.note: Explains that the doorway construction is made to enter this sleeping chamber. The reference is back to Nando, and the historical pera is preserved.

runs.text: Em qualquer hora, ou em todo

lines.note: Nandoqimo means at any hour or at all times. The scan supports the q in the time expression despite local abrasion.
Completes em todo o tempo, 'at all times'. The row belongs to the adverbial time expression immediately above.
Nandoqi naritomo receives the same 'at any time' meaning. The printed space before naritomo is retained.
Nangan is glossed as great danger, hardship, or affliction. The enlarged letter sequence supports aflição rather than OCR aftição; no terminal stop is invented at the right edge.
Nangi is the second-person pronoun, glossed Tu and marked for written usage by upright S. It is a separate entry from the following difficult-to-govern adjective.

Nangi, explained as Voſamegataxi, describes something hard to govern or manage. The scan's initial N corrects the OCR headword Xangi; Japanese context and the repeated entry form support the distinction.

runs.text: ſe gouernar. ¶ Item, De ſarar, como do-

lines.note: Completes the governing sense, then extends it to difficulty in healing. Do- begins doença below; the extension is part of the same entry.
Completes doença and supplies Nangino yamai as the example of a difficult illness. The Portuguese translation begins on this row and specifies the difficulty below.
Completes the illness gloss as hard to cure or heal. Ruim describes the difficulty of recovery here, rather than identifying a particular disease.
Nangiô asks what subject or point is at issue. The scan supports separation of Que materia; its second interrogative use is introduced by Item and continued below.
Gives the additional interrogative sense 'how, or why?' This row concludes Nangiô and is not an independent headword.

Nanguen nango denotes gentle words or speech, matching Yauaracana cotoba. The damaged first letter of nango is read as n rather than OCR r; the surviving traces and repeated soft-speech construction support that choice, though the letter remains weak.
Completes Palauras and gives 'gentle conversation' as an alternative. The upright S. marks written usage separately from the italic Portuguese gloss.
Nangui means danger or affliction. Nanguini begins an example of coming into such adversity, whose verb is on the next physical row.

runs.text: Verſe em grande perigo, ou aflição.

lines.note: Completes Nanguini voyobu, finding oneself in great danger or affliction. Aflição restores the missing f from OCR alição; the small terminal stop is visible before the rule.
Nanguini vǒ is encountering danger or hardship. The marked vǒ form is preserved rather than modernized; the Portuguese object continues below.
Completes 'encounter some dangerous thing'. The line closes the second example of Nangui.
Nanguina is the corresponding adjective, dangerous and troublesome. The scan supports the full word despite weak ink in its opening letters.
Nanguini is explicitly labeled as the adverbial form. Its indented placement links it typographically to Nanguina without merging the two physical rows.
Nanguiſa is the nominal form for difficulty or hardship. It is printed alone on the final indented body row; no Portuguese gloss or missing continuation is supplied.

Nanguiǒ is a difficult observance or great penance, matching Cataqi voconai. The visible terminal hyphen is restored; the faint mark above the last e is read provisionally as the nasal abbreviation ẽ, completed by cia below.
Completes penitẽcia and supplies 'hardship' as an alternative. The source abbreviation is not expanded by adding an n to the canonical text.
The paired expression Nanguiǒ cuguiǒ receives the same penance or hardship meaning. Both printed carons are retained independently.
Nani is glossed 'what?' when addressing an inferior. The visible question mark replaces OCR Quee; the social-use qualification is the dictionary's own description.
Nanicaua expresses 'why?' or 'how?' with doubt. The historical Portuguese spelling Duuidando and the source's joined Porque are preserved.

runs.text: Tudo, ou por todas as vias.

lines.note: Nanifen is glossed as 'everything' or 'by every means'. The vowel after f is badly abraded: its surviving open lower curve favors e over OCR a, while the supplied NINJAL entry supports Nanifen. This applied reading remains uncertain because the upper part of the type is lost.
Nanifodono asks or expresses how great something is. Its attributive ending no and the unmarked Portuguese Quam are retained.
Nanigaxi can stand for an unnamed person or for the speaker. The example begins Quantôno; its circumflex and attached no remain part of the Japanese citation, not Portuguese typography candidates.
The example says that Toſabô from Quantô came up as an attacker against 'me'. This supports the first-person use of nanigaxi; the source's historical spelling and spacing are retained.

runs.text: O Bonzo Toſa do Quantou ſubio ao Mi-

lines.note: Toſ. is the upright source label. The Portuguese identifies the monk Toſa from Quantou and begins the divided capital-name Mi-yaco; these names occur within the Portuguese translation, unlike the preceding standalone Japanese sentence.
Completes Miyaco and the purpose 'to kill me'. The first-person Portuguese explicitly confirms the intended use of nanigaxi in the citation.
Nanigoto asks 'what thing'. The scan's crossed t restores the headword from OCR Nanigoio, with no need to change its printed spacing.
Nanigotomo is explained as nothing or no thing when used negatively. The lowercase com- begins commummente; the colon and nasal abbreviation in nenhũa are retained.

runs.text: mummente ſe vſa no negatiuo. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the statement that the expression is commonly used with a negative. Nani- begins the first example on the next physical row.
Completes the question Nanigotomo gozaranuca? The Portuguese asks whether there is anything new; the scan supplies a question mark after the Japanese, but no hyphen after the final no.

runs.text: uo. i, Como estais, ou que vai? ¶

lines.note: No plus uo completes nouo. The idiomatic explanation is 'how are you, or how goes it?' A new Nanigotomo example starts at the right edge.
Completes the negative prediction that there will be nothing shameful. Fazzucaxij and gozarumai form a coherent historical Japanese example; their spellings are preserved despite weak ink.
Mon. is the upright citation label. The translation confirms that nothing shameful will occur; auera retains the source's unaccented historical spelling.
The paired expression means everything or anything at all. The last vowel of cagotomo is read as damaged o, not OCR e; the close Portuguese qualquercouſa join remains as printed.
This Nanji is a dangerous or difficult matter, explicitly explained as Cataqi coto. Dif- begins the Portuguese adjective continued below.
Completes difficultoſa, 'difficult'. The divided word belongs to the preceding Nanji definition.

This Nanji denotes a difficult written character. The scan restores initial N from OCR Manji and the missing e in ler. The second pass confirms a visible gap before ler, while deſe remains tightly joined; the transcription is deſe ler rather than a modernized phrase.

runs.text: Nanji, zuru, ita. i, Nanuo yǔ.

lines.note: The verb Nanji, zuru, ita means finding fault or raising an objection, paraphrased as Nanuo yǔ. The scan supplies yǔ, not the OCR's malformed yiǔi, with the caron over u retained.
Completes the verb's senses: criticize, argue against, or put in doubt. The source's unaccented por is retained rather than silently converted to modern pôr.
Nanjin denotes a person from the southern regions, matching Minamino fito. The final n is visibly present and restores the letter omitted by OCR Nanji.
Completes 'from the south' and begins a saying about describing snow to a southerner and plums to a northerner. The scan reads ſul, not ſil, and shows no full stop after focujin at the line edge.

runs.text: Dizer couſas que ſe não en-

lines.note: Completes the second half of the saying, speaking of ume to a northerner. The Portuguese begins its figurative interpretation: saying things the listener does not understand.

runs.text: tendem: por que os do ſul não virão neue, nem

lines.note: Completes entendem and gives the dictionary's rationale about southerners not having seen snow. This historical explanation is transcribed as a source claim, not asserted as a universal geographical fact.

runs.text: os do norte Vmes, que ſão hũas certas ameixas.

lines.note: Adds the source's corresponding claim about northerners and Vmes, explained as a kind of plum. Vmes is the Japanese fruit-name inside Portuguese; the scan supports hũas rather than OCR hũae.
Nanimo is glossed 'everything' when joined to affirmative verbs. The grammatical qualification is essential to the contrast with the negative use below.
Completes afirmatiuos and gives Nanimo gozaru, 'everything is there'. Its Portuguese Tudo is completed by hà on the next row.

runs.text: hà. Cõ verbos negatiuos ſignifica nada, ou ne-

lines.note: Completes Tudo hà, then contrasts negative verbs, where the expression means nothing. The scan restores italic hà, abbreviated Cõ, and negatiuos from the garbled OCR; ne- begins nenhũa below.
Completes nenhũa couſa and gives Nanimo nai as the negative example, 'there is nothing'. The contraction and nasal marking remain in their printed positions.
Nanimo camo is an inclusive expression glossed simply 'everything'. The two printed Japanese words remain separated.
Naninani is an interrogative expression, 'what thing?' The repetition belongs to the headword and is not accidental duplication.
Naninaritomo means whatever thing it may be. The headword is printed as a single string, unlike the two-word expression Nanimo camo above.
Naninicaua asks 'what, or for what purpose?' Upright S. marks written usage, and Na- begins the following citation rather than a new entry.

Na- plus ua begins the quoted Japanese, apparently about a name circulating in the transient world. The Portuguese below paraphrases this differently, in terms of living in the miserable world; that source-level difference is preserved rather than harmonized.
Completes naninicaua xento, asking what use or purpose it would serve. Taif. is the upright source label and Lib. 30 gives the book; Ainda begins the Portuguese concessive translation.

runs.text: que agora viua no meo do mundo miſerauel que

lines.note: Continues the Portuguese paraphrase, 'although I now live in the midst of the miserable world'. Its final que introduces the question about benefit on the following row.
Completes the question, 'what benefit will it bring me?' The scan gives a single word aproueitarà with a grave accent and a question mark; the OCR's separated à and trailing ẽ are not printed text.

runs.text: Nanjo. Cataqi tocoro. i, Varui michi.

lines.note: Nanjo is a difficult place, explained further as a bad road. Ca begins Caminho across the row boundary, but the clear right-edge space contains no printed hyphen.

runs.text: minho trabalhoſo, como caminho de pedras,

lines.note: Completes Caminho and describes an arduous road, such as a stony one. Trabalhoſo replaces OCR trabalheſo, and the visible comma introduces the next example below.
Adds steep slopes or hillsides as examples of difficult roads. This continuation closes Nanjo.

runs.text: Nanino cano. i, Nanito xite cato xite.

lines.note: Nanino cano is explained by Nanito xite cato xite, an expression of assorted pretexts. The scan supports final xite rather than OCR xire; Mo starts Modo without a printed terminal hyphen.

runs.text: do deſe eſcuſar, & dizer varias couſas pera

lines.note: Completes Modo and describes excusing oneself by saying various things. The purpose clause continues below, and the close deſe spacing is preserved.

Completes the idea of getting oneself free of an obligation and gives Nanino canoto yǔte, 'saying this and that'. Liurar restores the small i missed by OCR; the next page continues the translation after the catchword Dizendo.
